novel_actions_proposed.label: diagnose_execution_vs_expectation
novel_actions_proposed.description: Before siding with either party, determine whether the complaint stems from execution drift (temperature, timing, finishing, holding) or a genuine mismatch between menu promise and guest expectation, then act accordingly.

novel_actions_proposed.label: stop_harm_then_audit_standards
novel_actions_proposed.description: Immediately restore the guest's experience and safety, then use the incident to hold kitchen standards accountable through a structured post-service review rather than choosing a winner in the moment.

novel_actions_proposed.label: tiered_service_recovery_with_learning
novel_actions_proposed.description: Implement fast service recovery for the guest first, then conduct a structured quality diagnosis afterward to distinguish execution failure from expectation mismatch, preserving both guest trust and chef authority.

synthesis_description: Rather than forcing a binary choice between siding with the customer or the chef, the manager should immediately remedy the guest's harm (apology, replacement, or alternative) while suspending judgment on fault, then conduct a structured post-incident review to distinguish execution drift from expectation mismatch—preserving both customer dignity and chef credibility without undermining either.
points_of_disagreement: How much immediate weight to give the customer's lived experience versus the chef's technical claim of correctness before any investigation.
Whether authenticity concerns can ever justify declining a service-recovery remedy, or whether guest restoration always takes precedence in the moment.
The degree to which the manager should visibly involve or consult the chef during the live service recovery, versus handling it entirely front-of-house first.
summary: All three agents converged on a novel synthesis that rejects the original binary framing (side with customer vs. side with chef). They uniformly propose a two-phase approach: (1) enact immediate, dignified service recovery for the guest without pre-judging fault, and (2) conduct a structured post-service diagnosis to determine whether the failure was execution drift or an expectation mismatch—thereby protecting guest trust, chef credibility, and kitchen accountability simultaneously. The main tensions not fully resolved concern how much real-time transparency to give the chef during recovery and whether authenticity can ever override a remedy obligation.
